stem: A 55-year-old male presents with fever, chills, and flank pain. Laboratory tests show pyuria, bacteremia, and evidence of sepsis. Imaging reveals a 6-mm obstructing ureteric stone. What is the most appropriate management?
srcNote: Other source key (Final 429 F Q86 (p. 297)): A 20 year old man presented with left flank pain and fever. CT scan showed 4 mm stone in the mid ureter. What is the appropriate next step? B. Antibiotics and double J stunting. B (Investigation of Urinary tract Problems & Renal Colic)
expl: Sepsis with an obstructing stone = an infected, obstructed kidney → urgent decompression plus IV antibiotics (after cultures). Antibiotics can't reach an undrained kidney; the stone is treated later, once the infection clears.

why.A: Oral antibiotics and observation risk fatal urosepsis.
why.B: A stent also decompresses, but on its own (no antibiotics) it isn't the full answer; in a septic patient a nephrostomy under local anaesthesia is often preferred.
why.D: Treating the stone in an infected obstructed system causes sepsis.

stem: A 40-year-old male presents with severe flank pain. Imaging shows a ureteric stone with hydronephrosis. He is stable, with no signs of infection. What is the most appropriate management?
expl: A stable patient with a ureteric stone and no infection can have definitive stone treatment; of the options only ESWL is a stone treatment (URS, not offered, is preferred lower in the ureter).

why.A: Nephrectomy is for a non-functioning kidney, not a stone.
why.C: Open surgery is almost never needed now.
why.D: There is no infection, and antibiotics don't treat a stone.

stem: Pt presented will renal stones, what is the investigation of choice?
srcNote: (Investigation of Urinary tract Problems & Renal Colic) Source note (Final 441 A Q11): Patient present with acute flank pain that radiates to the groin what is the gold standard investigation? CT Abdomen and pelvis without contrast
expl: Non-contrast CT (CT KUB) is the gold standard for urinary stones — it shows virtually all stones (including radiolucent uric acid), their size and site, and alternative diagnoses.

why.A: KUB misses radiolucent stones.
why.D: IVP needs contrast and has been replaced by CT.

stem: A patient presents with flank pain radiating to the groin , hematuria, and recurrent urinary tract infections (UTIs). Urine analysis reveals alkaline pH and the presence of bacteria with urease activity.What type of stone is most likely present in this patient?
expl: Recurrent UTIs with urease-producing bacteria (Proteus) and alkaline urine → struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) "infection stones", which can grow into staghorn calculi.

why.A: Calcium oxalate is the commonest stone but isn't linked to urease organisms.
why.B: Uric acid forms in acidic urine.
why.D: Calcium phosphate forms in alkaline urine but not from urease bacteria.

stem: What is the diagnosis?
srcNote: Choices C and D are incomplete in the source. The original wording of choices A and B is preserved.
expl: The coronal non-contrast CT shows a bright (high-density) stone in the left kidney — a kidney stone.

why.A: Correct.

stem: A 25 year old healthy man presented to the emergency department with 2 days of history of recurrent attacks of left ureteric colic. Intravenous urogram confirmed the presence of 4mm radio-opaque stone in the left distal ureter. Which of the following is the initial management?
srcNote: (Investigation of Urinary tract Problems & Renal Colic)
expl: A small (4 mm) distal ureteric stone in a healthy man without infection or renal impairment will usually pass → analgesia (NSAIDs), hydration ± medical expulsive therapy (tamsulosin).

why.A: Correct.
why.D: Cystoscopy doesn't treat a ureteric stone.

stem: A 45-year-old man was diagnosed with left renal stone. His KUB x-ray is shown below. Which one of the following is the best treatment option?
srcNote: (Investigation of Urinary tract Problems & Renal Colic) Source note (Final 438 F Q21): staghorn stone management? A. PCNL A (Investigation of Urinary tract Problems & Renal Colic)
expl: A large branched (staghorn) renal stone (> 2 cm) is treated by percutaneous nephrolithotomy.

why.A: ESWL is for renal stones < 2 cm.
why.C: A staghorn stone won't respond to medical treatment.
why.D: Correct.

stem: A 55-year-old man with a history of one pack cigarettes smoking daily for 40 years. He complained of occasional gross painless hematuria. Which of the following is the next step of management?
expl: Painless gross haematuria in a heavy smoker over 40 → evaluate for urothelial cancer: CT urography for the upper tracts (plus cystoscopy).

why.A: IVU is the older, less sensitive test.
why.B: US can miss small urothelial tumours.
why.D: Correct.

stem: A 25 year-old woman presented to the emergency department with left flank pain. CT revealed 6 mm left ureteric stone. What is the management?
srcNote: Source key was A; corrected — see explanation. (Investigation of Urinary tract Problems & Renal Colic)
expl: A 6-mm ureteric stone with no infection, renal impairment, intractable pain or vomiting is uncomplicated colic → the doctor's pathway is conservative: hydration, analgesia and medical expulsive therapy, intervening only for an indication (infection, renal impairment, persistent nausea/vomiting, pain not controlled orally, failure of medical therapy). The source key (ureteroscopy) fits only if one of those is present.

why.A: Definitive treatment when an indication exists or MET fails.
why.B: Stents are for an obstructed infected kidney or renal impairment.
why.D: Also an intervention without an indication.

stem: Woman post MVA. What's the most likely diagnosis?
expl: On the cystogram the contrast escapes around the bladder in the pelvis (flame-shaped, not outlining bowel) → extraperitoneal bladder rupture, typical with pelvic fractures; managed with catheter drainage.

why.A: A urethral injury shows extravasation at the urethra on a urethrogram.
why.D: Intraperitoneal rupture outlines bowel loops and paracolic gutters.

stem: A 60-year-old man with history of one pack cigarettes smoking daily for 40 years. He presented complain of occasional gross painless hematuria. The urine test reveals no UTI and the CT urogram is normal. Which of the following is the next step of management?
srcNote: (Investigation of Urinary tract Problems & Renal Colic)
expl: Painless haematuria in a smoker needs the upper tracts AND the bladder assessed; a normal CT urogram doesn't exclude a flat bladder tumour → cystoscopy.

why.A: IVP adds nothing after CT.
why.D: Correct.

stem: A 30-year-old man was involved in a motor vehicle accident and was diagnosed with left grade 3 renal trauma which was managed successfully. 3 weeks later, he presented with hematuria and left renal colic with no other symptoms. Physical examination was unremarkable.Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis ?
srcNote: Source key was A; corrected — see explanation. (Investigation of Urinary tract Problems & Renal Colic)
expl: Delayed haematuria 2–3 weeks after conservatively managed renal trauma is the classic presentation of a renal artery pseudoaneurysm (or AV fistula); passing clots causes colic. Diagnose with CT angiography and treat by angio-embolization. The source key (renal stone) doesn't fit the timing after trauma.

why.A: Stones don't form in 3 weeks; this follows the injury.
why.B: There is no fever or sign of infection.
why.D: Incomplete healing doesn't cause a new bleed after a quiet interval — a pseudoaneurysm does.

stem: Female patient underwent emergency hysterectomy. 2 days post op the wound drains (clear fluid) 800ml/24h and the urethra 700ml/24h. What is the most likely cause?
expl: 800 mL/day of clear fluid from the drain plus only 700 mL/day of urine after hysterectomy → urine leaking from an injured ureter (one kidney drains into the abdomen).

why.A: Correct.
why.B: Bladder injury would reduce urethral urine more and show haematuria.
why.D: Would give blood.

stem: A 60-year-old male patient presented with gross painless haematuria. His urine analysis showed uncountable RBCs. What best explains this patient's presentation?
expl: Painless gross haematuria in a 60-year-old = urothelial carcinoma (bladder) until proven otherwise.

why.A: Correct.
why.B: Malaria (blackwater fever) causes haemoglobinuria, not RBCs in the urine.
why.C: Wilms tumour is a childhood tumour.
why.D: Beetroot colours the urine red without RBCs.

stem: How is the most reliable urine specimen to diagnose urinary tract infection (UTI) obtained?
srcNote: MSU is the most commonly used, suprapubic aspiration is the most reliable but not used because it is invasive (Investigation of Urinary tract Problems & Renal Colic)
expl: Suprapubic aspiration bypasses the urethra, so it is the most reliable (least contaminated) specimen — any growth is significant.

why.A: Midstream urine is routine but can be contaminated.
why.B: Catheterization is less contaminated than midstream, but less reliable than suprapubic aspiration.
why.D: A sample from an existing catheter is often colonized.

stem: a 7-year-old boy sustained a straddle injury while jumping with his bike. He had urethral bleeding and difficulty in voiding. What is the next step in managing this patient?

opts.t: Stop the bleeding by penile compression
Insert urethral foley catheter to relief his urine retention

srcNote: Source key was B; corrected — see explanation. (Investigation of Urinary tract Problems & Renal Colic)
expl: Straddle injury + blood at the meatus + difficulty voiding = urethral injury (bulbar) → retrograde (ascending) urethrogram first; never blind catheterization (suprapubic catheter if retention). The source keyed penile compression, which isn't the management.

why.A: Exploration is for complete rupture after imaging.
why.D: Catheterization can convert a partial tear into a complete one.

stem: A 40 year old man presented to the ER with sudden onset right flank pain, radiating to the lower abdomen. His exam reveals costovertebral angle tenderness. What is the most likely possible cause of his pain?
srcNote: Source key was AB; corrected — see explanation. (Investigation of Urinary tract Problems & Renal Colic)
expl: Sudden, severe flank pain radiating to the lower abdomen/groin with CVA tenderness is renal (ureteric) colic — caused by a stone obstructing the ureter. The source listed both A and B; a non-obstructing kidney stone usually doesn't give colic.

why.A: A kidney stone causes colic only when it obstructs the PUJ — less typical than a ureteric stone.
why.C: A bladder stone causes suprapubic pain and voiding symptoms.
why.D: Gallstones cause right upper quadrant pain, not CVA tenderness radiating down.

stem: A woman came for routine check up for employment and her urine was turbid with high WBCs and negative culture.
srcNote: Incomplete source recall; the question prompt is not provided after the clinical statement. Source note (Final 433 F Q1 (p. 188)): Answer: A (incomplete?)
expl: Sterile pyuria (WBCs with a negative culture) suggests TB, stones or a tumour; of the options, tumour fits.

why.A: Correct.
why.B: Stricture causes obstructive symptoms; infections it causes grow on culture.
why.C: Retention isn't diagnosed from urinalysis and causes infected urine.
why.D: Trauma causes haematuria, not pyuria.

stem: A 25 YO man present to the ER with severe sudden right flank pain radiating to the lower abdomen associated with frequency and urgency. After controlling his pain Ultrasound is done revealing a 1 cm stone in the right kidney pelvis. The plain X-ray KUB did not reveal any stone over the renal area. Which one of the following is the most probable stone composition in this patient?
srcNote: (Investigation of Urinary tract Problems & Renal Colic)
expl: A stone seen on US but invisible on KUB is radiolucent → uric acid (or xanthine).

why.A: Calcium phosphate is radio-opaque.
why.D: Struvite is faintly radio-opaque.

stem: 30 year old man presenting after MVA” motor vehicle accident”. The patient has blood at the urethral meatus. What is the most appropriate next step?
srcNote: (Investigation of Urinary tract Problems & Renal Colic)
expl: Blood at the urethral meatus = urethral injury until proven otherwise → retrograde urethrogram before any catheter.

why.A: Contraindicated before imaging.
why.C: Suprapubic if a urethrogram shows disruption and he can't void.
why.D: Correct.

stem: A 55 year old man presented with painless macroscopic haematuria. Which of the Following is the imaging modality of choice?
expl: Painless haematuria needs upper-tract imaging; in this older key the choice is intravenous urography. Today it is CT urography (not offered), plus cystoscopy.

why.A: US can miss small urothelial tumours.
why.D: Isotope scans show function, not tumours.

stem: A 55 year old lady was diagnosed to have a solid 6 cm left renal mass with no evidence of metastasis and a normal contralateral kidney on work up. Which ONE of the following is the most appropriate management?

opts.t: Neo-adjuvant chemotherapy followed by partial nephrectomy

expl: A localized solid renal mass (RCC) with a normal opposite kidney → surgical removal; radical nephrectomy is the answer here (partial nephrectomy is preferred when technically feasible, but never after neoadjuvant chemotherapy).

why.A: RCC is chemo-resistant.
why.D: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy has no role in RCC.
